explanations.A: Non-invasive ventilation delivered as BiPAP is the established first-line therapy for a COPD exacerbation complicated by hypercapnic respiratory acidosis. The inspiratory pressure augments alveolar ventilation so carbon dioxide is washed out, while the expiratory pressure offsets intrinsic PEEP and relieves the work of breathing. Early NIV lowers intubation rates, hospital stay and mortality.
explanations.B: Intubation and invasive ventilation are held in reserve for patients who cannot tolerate NIV, who have a depressed sensorium or unprotected airway, or who continue to deteriorate on a trial of non-invasive support. questions.question: A nurse teaches the mother of an infant with cleft lip and palate to use a specialised feeding bottle. A standard bottle with an enlarged teat hole
questions.explanation: The Haberman (SpecialNeeds) feeder is the device described: an elongated compressible teat holding a milk reservoir, a slit valve at the tip that can be rotated to three flow settings, and a one-way valve at the base that stops milk running back into the bottle. explanations.A: The Haberman (SpecialNeeds) feeder is the device described: an elongated compressible teat holding a milk reservoir, a slit valve at the tip that can be rotated to three flow settings, and a one-way valve at the base that stops milk running back into the bottle. questions.question: While a patient is being repositioned, the chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the pleural space. Which nursing action should be taken immediately?
options: Immerse the tube end in sterile saline
Apply an airtight dressing
Clamp the chest tube
Encourage deep breathing
questions.explanation: The open chest wound must be sealed at once, because atmospheric air is being sucked into the pleural space with every breath. The nurse covers the site with a sterile occlusive dressing such as petroleum gauze, secures it on three sides so trapped air can still escape rather than build up into a tension pneumothorax, then stays with the patient, monitors respiration and saturation, and summons the physician for reinsertion and a chest radiograph.

explanations.A: Placing the end under water is the correct response when the drainage system disconnects but the tube is still in the chest. It has no place once the tube is out of the patient, and reinserting a contaminated tube risks empyema.
